opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I try not to over-structure it, but there are a few habits I've settled into over time.

The mornings are the most precious part of my day, so I protect them for deep thinking. That's when I do the hardest work: reading papers carefully, working through a problem, or writing. I try not to check messages or schedule meetings before noon if I can avoid it, because once that context-switching starts, it's very hard to get back into a focused state.

The afternoons are more collaborative. That's when I meet with colleagues, talk through ideas, review experiments, and give feedback. A lot of good research comes out of those conversations. Someone pokes a hole in your idea, or mentions something from a different area that suddenly connects. So I don't see that time as less important, just a different mode.

I also try to leave some unstructured time, maybe going for a walk or just thinking without a specific goal. Some of my better ideas came when I wasn't actively trying to solve anything. In research it's tempting to measure productivity by hours at the desk, but I've learned that's not really how insight works.

And then I try to end the day by writing a few notes on where I am and what I want to pick up tomorrow. It sounds small, but it makes the next morning much easier to start, and it keeps me from carrying everything around in my head all evening.

It's not perfect, and some weeks deadlines take over everything. But that's roughly the rhythm I aim for.

r001.rationale: The response says Kay protects mornings for deep thinking and avoids messages or meetings before noon, but it does not say she works from home before going to the office or describe that routine as “cave time.”

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I've stopped pretending I can plan a research day the way you'd plan a factory shift. What I do instead is protect one thing: a long, uninterrupted block in the morning, usually three or four hours, where I'm not in meetings and I'm not on Slack. That block is for whatever is hardest right now. Sometimes that's reading a paper carefully, sometimes it's writing, sometimes it's just sitting with a result that doesn't make sense and refusing to look away from it.

The reason I'm strict about that block is that research progress tends to be lumpy. You can go a week with nothing, and then the whole thing clicks in an afternoon. But that afternoon only happens if you've been loading the problem into your head consistently. If I fragment the morning into half-hour pieces, I never get deep enough for the click to happen.

Afternoons are more social and more reactive. That's when I meet with students or collaborators, run experiments I've already designed, answer email, review things. I find those tasks actually benefit from having a slightly tired brain, because I'm less tempted to over-engineer them.

The other habit I'd mention is that I end the day by writing down the very next concrete thing to do, not a to-do list, just one sentence. "Rerun the ablation with the smaller learning rate." "Figure out why Figure 3 disagrees with Table 2." It sounds trivial, but it removes the cold-start problem the next morning. You sit down and you already know where to put your hands.

And I try to leave some slack. If every hour is accounted for, there's no room for the accidental conversation or the tangent that turns out to matter. A lot of the best ideas I've had came from time that looked unproductive on a calendar.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes protecting an uninterrupted morning work block, but does not say Kay works from home before going to the office or call it solitary “cave time.”

astra-6.text: I like to give the day a little structure without planning every hour. I try to protect a block of quiet time for whatever needs the most concentration—reading, thinking through a problem, or writing. Then I group things like email and meetings together so they don’t keep interrupting that work. Research can be unpredictable, though, so I leave room to follow an interesting question. At the end of the day, I like to jot down where I’ve got to and what I want to try next. That makes it easier to pick things up the next morning.
